verses.text: Now the days of David came near that he should die; and he commanded Solomon his son, saying,
“I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man;

and keep the instruction of Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, his commandments, his ordinances, and his testimonies, according to that which is written in the law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do, and wherever you turn yourself.

Then Yahweh may establish his word which he spoke concerning me, saying, ‘If your children are careful of their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail you,’ he said, ‘a man on the throne of Israel.’

“Moreover you know also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, even what he did to the two captains of the armies of Israel, to Abner the son of Ner, and to Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, and shed the blood of war in peace, and put the blood of war on his sash that was around his waist, and in his shoes that were on his feet.
Do therefore according to your wisdom, and don’t let his gray head go down to Sheol  in peace.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table; for so they came to me when I fled from Absalom your brother.

“Behold, there is with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, of Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse in the day when I went to Mahanaim; but he came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by Yahweh, saying, ‘I will not put you to death with the sword.’
Now therefore don’t hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man; and you will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down to Sheol  with blood.”
David slept with his fathers, and was buried in David’s city.
The days that David reigned over Israel were forty years; he reigned seven years in Hebron, and he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Solomon sat on David his father’s throne; and his kingdom was firmly established.
Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. She said, “Do you come peaceably?” He said, “Peaceably.
He said moreover, I have something to tell you.” She said, “Say on.”

He said, “You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel set their faces on me, that I should reign. However the kingdom is turned around, and has become my brother’s; for it was his from Yahweh.
Now I ask one petition of you. Don’t deny me.” She said to him, “Say on.”
He said, “Please speak to Solomon the king (for he will not tell you ‘no’), that he give me Abishag the Shunammite as wife.”
Bathsheba said, “Alright. I will speak for you to the king.”

Bathsheba therefore went to king Solomon, to speak to him for Adonijah. The king rose up to meet her, and bowed himself to her, and sat down on his throne, and caused a throne to be set for the king’s mother; and she sat on his right hand.
Then she said, “I ask one small petition of you; don’t deny me.” The king said to her, “Ask on, my mother; for I will not deny you.”
She said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as wife.”

King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also; for he is my elder brother; even for him, and for Abiathar the priest, and for Joab the son of Zeruiah.”
Then king Solomon swore by Yahweh, saying, “God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life.
Now therefore as Yahweh lives, who has established me, and set me on my father David’s throne, and who has made me a house as he promised, surely Adonijah shall be put to death today.”
King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell on him, so that he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, “Go to Anathoth, to your own fields; for you are worthy of death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you bore the Lord  Yahweh’s ark before David my father, and because you were afflicted in all in which my father was afflicted.”
So Solomon thrust Abiathar out from being priest to Yahweh, that he might fulfill Yahweh’s word, which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.
This news came to Joab; for Joab had followed Adonijah, although he didn’t follow Absalom. Joab fled to Yahweh’s Tent, and held onto the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told, “Joab has fled to Yahweh’s Tent, and behold, he is by the altar.” Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go, fall on him.”

Benaiah came to Yahweh’s Tent, and said to him, “Thus says the king, ‘Come out!’” He said, “No; but I will die here.” Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, “Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me.”
The king said to him, “Do as he has said, and fall on him, and bury him; that you may take away the blood, which Joab shed without cause, from me and from my father’s house.

Yahweh will return his blood on his own head, because he fell on two men more righteous and better than he, and killed them with the sword, and my father David didn’t know it: Abner the son of Ner, captain of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the army of Judah.

So their blood will return on the head of Joab, and on the head of his offspring  forever. But for David, for his offspring,  for his house, and for his throne, there will be peace forever from Yahweh.”
Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and fell on him, and killed him; and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his place over the army; and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, and live there, and don’t go anywhere else.
For on the day you go out and pass over the brook Kidron, know for certain that you will surely die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
Shimei said to the king, “What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do.” Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.
At the end of three years, two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. They told Shimei, saying, “Behold, your slaves are in Gath.”
Shimei arose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to Achish, to seek his slaves; and Shimei went, and brought his slaves from Gath.
Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and had come again.

The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Didn’t I adjure you by Yahweh, and warn you, saying, ‘Know for certain, that on the day you go out, and walk anywhere else, you shall surely die?’ You said to me, ‘The saying that I have heard is good.’
Why then have you not kept the oath of Yahweh, and the commandment that I have instructed you with?”
The king said moreover to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the wickedness that you did to David my father. Therefore Yahweh will return your wickedness on your own head.
But king Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be established before Yahweh forever.”
So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he went out, and fell on him, so that he died. The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.

footnotes.content: David knows his time is ending. Not with panic or denial, but with clear eyes—he calls his son near and begins to pass on what he has learned. When we sense a season closing, do we gather the ones we love and tell them what matters most?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Show yourself a man"—Solomon hears not a demand for toughness, but a call to maturity and steadiness. It's David's way of saying: gather your strength, carry what is true, and lead with the weight of covenant. The kingdom requires more than youth; it needs a man rooted in something larger than himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David plants the law of Moses at the center of Solomon's reign. The instruction—the Torah, the statutes, commandments, ordinances, testimonies—is not a burden Solomon must drag along, but the very soil where his prosperity will grow. Obedience and blessing are not separate; they are one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the covenant promise to David: his sons will not lack a man on Israel's throne—but only if they walk before the Lord in truth, with whole heart and soul. It's not automatic inheritance; it's conditional on the next generation's faithfulness. Every promise of God carries with it the weight of our response.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David lifts the veil on Joab—the general who killed in peacetime, making war bloodguilt look like an accident. A son needs to see his father plain: not everything his hero did was heroic. Joab served David well in battle, but he crossed a line David cannot overlook.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace"—David's not telling Solomon to kill Joab outright, but to settle this debt of blood wisely. The old man will not escape the reckoning for the innocent blood he shed. Injustice may wear age gracefully, but the Lord sees every stain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But David also says: remember Barzillai. He brought bread and supplies when you fled from Absalom, when everything was crumbling. Show his sons kindness; let them eat at your table. A good king remembers both the debt of blood and the grace of loyalty. Both matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei—a Benjamite who cursed David as he fled to Mahanaim, yet later came down to meet him at the Jordan with reconciliation. David swore not to kill him by the sword, honoring his oath. But Solomon must know the truth of the man behind the amnesty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Don't hold him guiltless." David bound his own hands with an oath, but he is not binding Solomon's. His son must use wisdom to settle what David himself left unfinished. Sometimes a father's mercy opens a door for his son's justice. Both trust the same God to see what is right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David slept with his fathers and was buried in David's city—the same Jerusalem where he had ruled, where the Lord had made His name dwell. In death, even the great king returns to dust; but his city endures, and his throne, by God's covenant mercy, passes to his son.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years—seven in Hebron, thirty-three in Jerusalem. A long reign, and in that span David had seen Israel rise from dust to strength. The years accumulate, and what seemed new in youth becomes history. Solomon inherits not just a throne, but the weight of forty years of covenant work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon sat on his father's throne; his kingdom was firmly established. Not because he seized it or fought for it, but because the Lord had promised it and the people accepted it. The throne was ready; now Solomon must grow into it. Authority without character is a trap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah comes to Bathsheba—not with swords, but with words. He greets her as a suppliant, asking if he comes in peace. She senses something; she asks him to speak. In a court full of power plays, a mother's ear is often the first to hear what a son really wants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have something to tell you." Adonijah takes his time. He knows Bathsheba has Solomon's ear in a way few do. A man planning to ask for much begins by setting the stage, speaking softly, drawing a listener in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adonijah speaks truth twisted by bitterness: the kingdom was his by right, all Israel looked to him—but it turned and became Solomon's because it came from Yahweh. He sees the hand of God in it, yet cannot release the hurt of his own eclipse. When we see God's will cross our wishes, do we accept or resent?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I ask one petition of you. Don't deny me." Adonijah sounds humble, but he is testing the waters. He wants to know: will this queen intervene for him? Will she use her influence as his advocate? He has seen Solomon's respect for her; he is counting on it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let Abishag the Shunammite be my wife." It sounds innocent—an old man's aging widow, a companionship—but it is a power play. A man who marries a king's woman, even one who came late, touches the royal succession. Bathsheba, for a moment, does not see the edge of what he is asking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bathsheba says yes without hesitation. She hears a sad son asking for an old woman's care and says nothing to stop him. A mother's compassion can blind her to a son's cunning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon rises to meet her, bows, and sits her at his right hand—the place of highest honor. See what a king's mother holds: the power to call him to his feet, the right to sit beside him. It is a portrait of deep filial respect and of the role a wise king grants his mother in the kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Ask on, my mother; for I will not deny you." Solomon makes a vow—and the words are sincere. Yet they are also a trap he sets for himself. He has not asked what Bathsheba wants; he has only promised to give it. Wisdom would have been to listen first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bathsheba speaks the petition: let Abishag be given to Adonijah. She still does not see what it means. Or perhaps by now she does, and she is caught—she cannot withdraw her son's request without shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's eyes open. "Why do you ask this for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also; for he is my elder brother." Solomon sees it now—the game beneath the game. If Adonijah marries the last wife of King David, he touches a claim to the throne. Solomon names Abiathar the priest and Joab too; Adonijah has gathered men who want the old days back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah has not spoken this word against his own life." Solomon swears an oath—not in anger, but in terrible clarity. He has just realized his older brother is not reconciled; he is plotting still. The oath falls like a sentence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As Yahweh lives, who has established me and set me on my father David's throne, and who has made me a house as he promised, surely Adonijah shall be put to death today." Solomon grounds his judgment in God's promise—not in his own wounded pride. He is defending the throne the Lord gave him. There is a hard mercy in this, and a warning to anyone who would use intimacy as cover for rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah—Solomon's trusted agent—goes out and carries out the sentence. Adonijah dies. A chapter of David's household closes. Solomon has passed his first test as king: he saw the trap, did not fall into it, and removed the threat to his kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abiathar the priest—who had been with David, who bore the ark—is spared death but stripped of his office. Solomon honors the man's past service but removes him from power, because Abiathar sided with Adonijah. Mercy and justice do not always look like mercy from the one who receives it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon thrust Abiathar out "that he might fulfill Yahweh's word, which he spoke concerning the house of Eli." What Solomon does in his justice matches what the Lord has already decreed—a sign that his throne stands in harmony with God's will. The Lord's word, spoken through Samuel generations before, now comes to pass.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab hears the news—Adonijah is dead, Abiathar is removed—and he understands. Joab had followed Adonijah too. He runs to the tent of the Lord, grabs the horns of the altar, seeking sanctuary. A man who has shed blood without cause now seeks shelter in the house of God, hoping the altar will protect him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon is told where Joab hides. The king does not hesitate. He sends Benaiah with the same command: go, fall on him. The altar will not stay Solomon's hand. Blood debt does not dissolve in sanctuary; it must be reckoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah comes and calls: "Come out!" But Joab refuses. "No; but I will die here." A man who has lived by the sword and shed blood without cause now chooses to die before the altar. He will not come out. He will not kneel before Solomon. He will face death on his own ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon tells Benaiah: fall on him and bury him in his own house in the wilderness. This takes away the blood-debt from David's house and from Solomon's kingdom. Joab's death cleanses the throne. Solomon is learning that a king sometimes must do what is hard in order to make things clean.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh will return Joab's blood on his own head, because he killed two men more righteous and better than himself—Abner and Amasa—and David did not know it. The judgment is just: Joab is held accountable for blood he shed secretly. There are no hidden deeds before God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bloodshed will return on Joab's head and his offspring forever; but for David, his offspring, his house, and his throne, there will be peace forever from Yahweh. Solomon's hard mercy in settling these blood-debts is not cruelty; it is the purchase of peace for David's line. Sometimes righteousness requires a painful cut to stop the bleeding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah goes up to the tent, falls on Joab, and kills him. Joab dies where he sought refuge. There is a terrible irony in it: the man who shed blood without cause, who thought the altar would shelter him, finds no shelter there. God's mercy is not the same as man's evasion of justice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon puts Benaiah in Joab's place as commander of the army and puts Zadok the priest where Abiathar was. A new generation takes the offices of the old. Solomon is reshaping the kingdom according to his own judgment—and according to the Lord's covenant word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon calls for Shimei—the Benjamite who cursed David—and sets a boundary: build yourself a house in Jerusalem and live there. Don't go anywhere else. It is a mercy: not death, but exile within the city. Solomon remembers David's oath not to kill him by the sword, and he keeps that oath—but he also contains him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "On the day you cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you will die. Your blood will be on your own head." Solomon sets a boundary in the land, not in time. Step outside this line, and the oath is broken. Shimei is a man on probation, his life held in balance by his own obedience to a line drawn on the earth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei accepts the terms: "What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." He bows to Solomon's wisdom. For now, he is contained; for now, he accepts the boundary. A reprieve is not a pardon, but to the one who receives it, it is a second chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three years pass. Shimei's servants run away to Gath, and they tell him where. Time eases fear; memory fades. Shimei hears the news of his slaves and forgets—or chooses to forget—the boundary Solomon set. A reprieve tests whether we have learned obedience or merely postponed disobedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei saddled his donkey and went to Gath to seek his slaves. He crossed the boundary. Perhaps he thought three years had softened Solomon's memory; perhaps he thought his slaves mattered more than a king's word. Either way, he broke the oath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon is told that Shimei has gone from Jerusalem to Gath and come back. The king knows. Nothing escapes the notice of a vigilant throne. A servant watches, a report comes, and what was hidden is revealed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon calls for Shimei and reminds him of the oath: "Didn't I adjure you by Yahweh, and warn you? Know for certain that on the day you go out, you shall surely die. You said to me, 'The word I have heard is good.'" Solomon does not raise his voice; he simply speaks the truth. Shimei himself said he understood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why then have you not kept the oath of Yahweh, and the commandment that I have instructed you with?" The question hangs in the air like a gavel. Solomon has named it: the boundary was not Solomon's whim; it was a commandment, a covenant word. Shimei has broken it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You know in your heart all the wickedness that you did to David my father. Therefore Yahweh will return your wickedness on your own head." Solomon reaches back to Shimei's crime—the cursing of David—and names it. The reprieve did not erase the past; it suspended it. Now it falls due.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "But king Solomon will be blessed, and David's throne will be established before Yahweh forever." Even as Shimei faces judgment, Solomon speaks the promise that undergirds it all. The king's mercy and the king's judgment both serve the same God and the same throne. Neither is random; both flow from covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon commanded Benaiah, and he fell on Shimei; and he died. The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon. A reader today hears an echo: when we accept God's boundaries and then cross them anyway, we pay a price. Solomon's consolidation is complete—not through cruelty, but through the honest settlement of old debts. As of 2026-10, we can see how a kingdom at peace requires that justice and mercy walk together, and that leaders sometimes bear the weight of hard decisions so their people can rest secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
